step1_summary: Chief complaint: Soreness, cracking and dryness of the skin on the hands (palms), with intermittent itching; interfering with work.

Symptoms: Onset 3–4 months ago after a job change; progressive; now painful enough to miss work for the past 3 days; intermittently itchy; has bled when scratched; generalized mild dry skin on legs reported; tried E45 emollient and an oral antihistamine without improvement.
Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Medications / Allergies: Metformin; no known drug allergies.

Family / social history: Family history of diabetes; no known family skin disease. Social: works as a hotel housekeeper (bathrooms/bedrooms/corridors), frequently uses cleaning products and often does not wear gloves; non-smoker; drinks a couple of pints/week.
Vital signs / exam findings: No vitals or physical exam findings recorded in the transcript. Patient reports no fever and is systemically well.

I: Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection of the palm): Chronic, scaly, fissured palmar dermatitis can be due to fungal infection; diabetes predisposes to fungal skin infections and chronicity (fits 3–4 month course).
Secondary bacterial infection (e.g., impetiginization): Cracked, scratched skin that sometimes bleeds can become secondarily infected and worsen symptoms.
N: Chronic cutaneous malignancy (e.g., Bowen disease/SCC in situ): Chronic scaly fissured lesions can rarely represent neoplasia when persistent and unresponsive to treatment (less likely but considered for chronic non-healing lesions).
D: Xerosis due to metabolic/ageing or dehydration (including diabetic xerosis): Generalized dry skin noted and patient reports poor hydration and diabetes, which can cause skin dryness and fissuring.
I2: Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational hand dermatitis): Frequent exposure to cleaning agents without gloves is a classic cause of irritant dermatitis presenting with dry, cracked, painful palms.

Allergic contact dermatitis from cleaning products or gloves (delayed-type hypersensitivity): Sensitization to a chemical in cleaning products, detergents, or rubber accelerators in gloves can produce pruritic, cracked palms.
C: Inherited palmoplantar keratoderma: Congenital keratoderma can cause fissuring and thickening of palms/soles but would usually have an earlier onset and family history (low likelihood here).
A: Palmar psoriasis (autoimmune): Psoriasis can present on the palms as well-demarcated scaling/fissured plaques and can be itchy/painful; may present in middle age.
Atopic eczema (if undiagnosed adult onset): History of generalized dry skin could reflect atopic diathesis with hand eczema exacerbated by irritants.
T: Occupational/frictional trauma to the palms: Repetitive mechanical irritation from work (gripping, scrubbing) can cause fissuring and hyperkeratosis of the palms.
E: Dermopathy related to diabetes / metabolic skin change: Diabetes-associated xerosis and impaired skin barrier can predispose to fissuring and secondary dermatitis.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Temporal correlation with job change 3–4 months ago doing hotel housekeeping, frequent use of cleaning products, admits she often does not wear gloves; palms are primarily affected with cracking, dryness and pain — classical for irritant contact dermatitis from detergents/chemicals.
supporting_evidence: Symptoms began ~3–4 months ago after switching to current housekeeping job.
Frequent exposure to bathroom cleaning products and admits not consistently wearing gloves.
Palmar distribution with dryness, cracking and pain interfering with work.
Failed simple emollient (E45) and oral antihistamine — irritant eczema often needs topical steroids and avoidance.
opposing_evidence: No direct exam documented (physician's diagnosis suggested rather than documented lesions).
No mention of acute erythema/blistering that might be seen in some irritant reactions (but chronic irritant dermatitis can be fissured).

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis to cleaning products or gloves
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Occupational exposure to multiple chemicals/rubber accelerators can cause delayed-type hypersensitivity with pruritus and fissuring on palms; onset after starting new exposures fits sensitization possible within months.
supporting_evidence: Work exposure to cleaning agents and new job shortly before onset.
Pruritus is a prominent symptom (allergic dermatitis is often itchy).
Palmar distribution consistent with contact allergen exposure.
opposing_evidence: Allergic contact dermatitis often shows more acute flare after specific exposures and may not improve with simple emollients, but no trial of topical steroid or patch testing yet to confirm.
No history of prior similar allergic skin disease or atopy documented.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Psoriasis can present on palms with fissuring and pain; middle-aged adult onset is possible. However absence of psoriasis elsewhere or family history reduces likelihood.
supporting_evidence: Chronic course of months with fissuring and scaling-like dryness could be consistent with palmar psoriasis.
Painful fissuring on palms is compatible with palmar psoriasis involvement.
opposing_evidence: No reported psoriatic plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp, or nail changes; patient denies prior skin disease.
Strong temporal relationship to occupational exposures favors contact dermatitis over psoriasis.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Tinea manuum (fungal infection of the palm)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: A chronic scaly, fissured palmar dermatitis can be dermatophyte infection; diabetes predisposes to fungal infections. Often unilateral or associated with athlete's foot, which was not asked/mentioned.
supporting_evidence: Chronicity (3–4 months) and scaling/cracking could represent tinea.
Diabetes is a risk factor for fungal infections.
opposing_evidence: Distribution described as palms/hands consistent, but no mention of characteristic ring-like or well-demarcated border or associated foot infection.
No trial of topical/oral antifungal therapy yet; empiric response to steroids (if given) would worsen fungal infection—no such response recorded.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Diabetes can cause generalized dry skin and predispose to fissuring; patient reports dry legs and poor hydration. However focal severe palmar symptoms temporally linked to occupational exposures make an external cause more likely.
supporting_evidence: History of type 2 diabetes and generalized dryness (legs) and reported poor hydration.
Diabetes can cause impaired skin barrier and fissuring.
opposing_evidence: Focal palmar predominance and onset after a job change with exposure to irritants points toward contact dermatitis rather than purely metabolic xerosis.
Diabetic xerosis alone would be less likely to cause painful, work-limiting localized palmar inflammation.
